catalog_quote: The Kman tone system has three phonetic tone heights marked as follows; High- ˊ Mid ˉ Low ˋ A macron (ˉ) over a vowel represents mid-tone and not length throughout this grammar. However, of these, only the mid-tone occurs on monosyllabic roots in isolation. However, strikingly, a three-way contrast on monosyllabic roots can be heard in sentence context, since the tone on the verb root may be any of the three heights in context. ... The underlying system consists of glide tones which can apply either to single segments but form a system of suprasegmental patterns applied to polysyllabic words and compounds. The glides so far identified are High-Mid, High-Low and Mid-Low ... Kman is a sesquisyllabic language of a type common in the SE Asian region. audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation and locator check out verbatim in the held Blench & Kri 2019 PDF/txt (sect. 2.3.1 pp. 25-26; 2.3.5 p. 29), and the record's negative claim (no occurrence of 'stress'/'accent') is confirmed by a full-text search for stress/accent over the full text. (2) The classification 'tonal, no word-stress rule stated' rests on a 2019 fieldwork grammar draft by the principal current researcher on Kman with a native-speaker co-author; it is the best English-language source and the latest description overall. The only fuller works are Chinese-language grammars of the Zayü (Geman) variety (Li Daqin 2002, 324 pp; Li Daqin 2019), which Blench read and criticises on tone; nothing seen suggests they would overturn a 'tonal' coding, though they might add a weak-presyllable statement that refines the domain note. sources.citation: Sastry, G. Devi Prasada (1985). Mishmi Grammar. Central Institute of Indian Languages.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online (also digitized at HathiTrust, search-only (in copyright))
sources.note: The description is of the Digaru dialect (= Taraon / Digaro-Mishmi, Glottolog diga1241), stated explicitly on p. 5; Miju (Kman) data were used only for 'verification and cross-checking' and no Miju-specific phonological statement is made. The author treats Idu, Digaru and Miju as dialects of one 'Mishmi' language, whereas Glottolog lists them as separate languages, so the tonal description cannot be credited to Kman. Relative to the catalog (Kman listed with an empty rule, no existing statements) the work is silent on Kman stress; it neither agrees nor contradicts.
